```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(eco)
  library(unmarked)
  library(AICcmodavg)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(plotly)
})
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
options(digits = 3)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")
```

A site either holds a species or it does not, and a survey either finds it or
does not. Those are two different coin flips, and one survey per site cannot
tell them apart: an undetected species and an absent species produce the same
zero. The single-season occupancy model (MacKenzie et al. 2002; Kéry and Royle
2016, chapter 10) separates the two by surveying each site more than once
within a window short enough that the true state cannot change. This page
walks through that model on one eco table, from fetch to goodness of fit, with
`unmarked` doing the fitting.

{{< include _caveat.qmd >}}

## Try it first

Sites are occupied with probability $\psi$. Each of $J$ surveys of an occupied
site detects the species with probability $p$; surveys of an empty site never
do. Drag the sliders and watch the amber strips: those are occupied sites the
surveys never found, which are the whole reason the model exists.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var ids = ["psi", "p", "j", "n"], el = {}, val = {};
  ids.forEach(function (k) { el[k] = document.getElementById("occ-" + k); val[k] = document.getElementById("occ-" + k + "-val"); });
  var grid = document.getElementById("occ-grid");
  var out = {};
  ["true", "naive", "enaive", "pstar", "cond", "missed", "j1"].forEach(function (k) { out[k] = document.getElementById("occ-" + k); });
  var z = [], y = [];

  function simulate() {
    var psi = +el.psi.value, p = +el.p.value, J = +el.j.value, n = +el.n.value;
    z = []; y = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      z[i] = Math.random() < psi ? 1 : 0;
      y[i] = [];
      for (var j = 0; j < J; j++) y[i][j] = (z[i] === 1 && Math.random() < p) ? 1 : 0;
    }
  }

  function draw() {
    var psi = +el.psi.value, p = +el.p.value, J = +el.j.value, n = +el.n.value;
    val.psi.textContent = "ψ = " + psi.toFixed(2);
    val.p.textContent = "p = " + p.toFixed(2);
    val.j.textContent = "J = " + J;
    val.n.textContent = "n = " + n;
    var html = "", nTrue = 0, nNaive = 0, nMissed = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      var any = y[i].indexOf(1) >= 0;
      nTrue += z[i]; if (any) nNaive++;
      var missed = z[i] === 1 && !any; if (missed) nMissed++;
      var when = [];
      y[i].forEach(function (v, j) { if (v) when.push(j + 1); });
      var title = "site " + (i + 1) + ": " + (z[i] ? "occupied" : "empty") +
        (any ? ", detected on survey " + when.join(", ") : ", never detected");
      html += '<div title="' + title + '" style="display:flex;gap:2px;padding:2px;border-radius:3px;border:2px solid ' +
        (missed ? "#c08a1e" : "transparent") + ';' + (missed ? 'background:repeating-linear-gradient(45deg,#fbf1dc 0 3px,#fff 3px 6px);' : '') + '">';
      for (var j = 0; j < J; j++) {
        html += '<span style="display:inline-block;width:11px;height:14px;border-radius:2px;' +
          (y[i][j] ? 'background:#1e8a5a;' : 'background:#ededea;border:1px solid #c9ccc8;box-sizing:border-box;') + '"></span>';
      }
      html += "</div>";
    }
    grid.innerHTML = html;
    var pstar = 1 - Math.pow(1 - p, J);
    var q = psi * Math.pow(1 - p, J);
    out["true"].textContent = (nTrue / n).toFixed(2) + "  (" + nTrue + "/" + n + ")";
    out.naive.textContent = (nNaive / n).toFixed(2) + "  (" + nNaive + "/" + n + ")";
    out.enaive.textContent = (psi * pstar).toFixed(2);
    out.pstar.textContent = pstar.toFixed(2);
    out.cond.textContent = (q / (q + 1 - psi)).toFixed(3);
    out.missed.textContent = nMissed + " of " + nTrue;
    if (J === 1) {
      var prod = psi * p;
      // another (psi, p) pair with the same product: push p to 0.95 and solve for psi
      var altP = Math.abs(p - 0.95) < 0.01 ? 0.5 : 0.95;
      var altPsi = prod / altP;
      out.j1.style.display = "block";
      out.j1.innerHTML = "With one survey the data are Bernoulli(ψ·p) and only the product ψ·p = " + prod.toFixed(3) +
        " is identified: ψ = " + altPsi.toFixed(2) + " with p = " + altP.toFixed(2) +
        " produces exactly the same distribution of detections as the sliders' ψ = " + psi.toFixed(2) + ", p = " + p.toFixed(2) + ".";
    } else {
      out.j1.style.display = "none";
    }
  }

  ids.forEach(function (k) { el[k].addEventListener("input", function () { simulate(); draw(); }); });
  document.getElementById("occ-resim").addEventListener("click", function () { simulate(); draw(); });
  simulate(); draw();
})();
</script>
```

Three things to notice. Naive occupancy converges on $\psi[1-(1-p)^J]$, not on
$\psi$, and the gap closes only as $J$ grows or $p$ is high. The conditional
probability that an all-zero site is occupied is what the model will later
hand back for every undetected site, and it is small only when
$(1-p)^J$ is small. And at $J = 1$ the simulator admits that it cannot
distinguish a common, cryptic species from a rare, conspicuous one.

## The model

Site $i$ carries a latent state $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$,

$$
z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i),
$$

and survey $j$ of site $i$ returns a detection $y_{ij}$ that is possible only
when the site is occupied,

$$
y_{ij} \mid z_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_i \, p_{ij}).
$$

Covariates enter on the logit scale at the level where they vary:
$\text{logit}(\psi_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}$ for things fixed
at a site, $\text{logit}(p_{ij}) = \mathbf{w}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol{\alpha}$
for things that change between surveys. Summing $z_i$ out gives the marginal
likelihood of one site's detection history $\mathbf{y}_i$, a zero-inflated
product of Bernoullis:

$$
L(\psi, p \mid \mathbf{y}_i) \;=\; \psi_i \prod_{j} p_{ij}^{y_{ij}} (1 - p_{ij})^{1 - y_{ij}} \;+\; (1 - \psi_i)\, \mathbb{1}\!\left[\textstyle\sum_j y_{ij} = 0\right].
$$

A site with at least one detection contributes only the first term, so it is
known to be occupied and its surveys inform $p$ alone. An all-zero site
contributes $\psi_i (1-p_{i\cdot})^{J} + 1 - \psi_i$, the mixture of "occupied
and missed every time" with "empty". Replicate surveys are what make the two
terms separable: among the detected sites, the pattern of ones and zeros
across surveys estimates $p$ with no reference to $\psi$, and once $p$ is
pinned the share of all-zero sites that must be occupied follows. With $J = 1$
there is no within-site pattern, the likelihood depends on $\psi p$ only, and
the model is unidentified.

## The data

The table is `kery_2008_willowtit_occ`: the Swiss breeding bird survey's
willow tit data that ship with `unmarked` and that Kéry and Royle use for the
MHB examples in chapters 10 and 11. There are 237 one-km² quadrats, each
surveyed up to three times in one breeding season, with elevation, forest
cover and transect length at the quadrat and the survey date and intensity at
each visit. All covariates are standardised in the source file. Reads are
pinned to eco version 10 so the numbers on this page do not move when the
warehouse grows.

```{r}
#| label: fetch
#| message: true
library(eco)
eco_set_version(10)
eco_info("kery_2008_willowtit_occ")
d <- eco_fetch("kery_2008_willowtit_occ")
d <- d[order(d$unit, d$occasion), ]
rownames(d) <- NULL
head(d)
```

One row per survey. The `unit_` columns are constant within a site and will
become `unmarked`'s site covariates; the `obs_` columns vary by survey and
become its observation covariates. `occasion` is the survey index within the
single primary period, and the standard requires a row to exist exactly when a
survey happened.

```{r}
#| label: shape
table(table(d$unit))
nrow(d)
237 * 3 - nrow(d)
```

Forty-six site-surveys were never made, so forty-two quadrats have two rows
and two have one. They have no rows at all rather than rows with `y = 0`,
because a survey that did not happen is not evidence of absence. This matters
for the likelihood above: an all-zero history over two surveys contributes
$\psi (1-p)^2 + 1 - \psi$, while the same site padded to three zeros would
contribute $\psi (1-p)^3 + 1 - \psi$ and claim an extra miss that never
occurred. When the long table is widened those cells must become `NA`, which
`unmarked` treats as not surveyed. `eco_to_unmarked()` does exactly that.

```{r}
#| label: umf
umf <- eco_to_unmarked(d)
sum(is.na(getY(umf)))
head(siteCovs(umf))
head(obsCovs(umf))
```

The prefixes are gone because the frame already encodes the level:
`siteCovs()` holds what was `unit_*`, `obsCovs()` holds what was `obs_*`, one
row per site-by-survey cell in the frame's order. Naive occupancy is the share
of sites with at least one detection.

```{r}
#| label: naive
Y <- getY(umf)
naive <- mean(rowSums(Y, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
naive
```

## Fit

`occu()` takes a double right-hand-side formula: detection first, occupancy
second. Three models: the null model; one that puts elevation and forest on
$\psi$ with a quadratic in elevation, since willow tits are a subalpine bird
and should peak at mid elevation; and one that adds survey date and intensity
on $p$.

```{r}
#| label: fit
m0 <- occu(~ 1 ~ 1, umf)
m1 <- occu(~ 1 ~ elev + I(elev^2) + forest, umf)
m2 <- occu(~ date_doy_std + ivel_std ~ elev + I(elev^2) + forest, umf)
modSel(fitList(null = m0, psi_covs = m1, psi_and_p_covs = m2))
```

```{r}
#| label: summary
summary(m2)
```

```{r}
#| label: est
#| echo: false
psi0 <- coef(backTransform(m0, "state"))
p0   <- coef(backTransform(m0, "det"))
b    <- coef(m2)
```

Occupancy rises steeply with elevation, turns over above the mean (the
quadratic term is negative), and is higher in forested quadrats. Neither
detection covariate earns its place: the AIC gain from `m1` to `m2` is below
what two free parameters cost, and both coefficients sit well inside their
standard errors. The null model's constants are the ones the simulator's
sliders correspond to.

```{r}
#| label: null-est
backTransform(m0, "state")
backTransform(m0, "det")
```

## Interpret

**Naive against estimated.** Under the null model $\hat\psi$ = `r fmt(psi0)`
against a naive `r fmt(naive)`, a correction of only `r fmt(psi0 - naive)`.
That is not a failure of the method. With $\hat p$ = `r fmt(p0)` per survey
the cumulative detection over three visits is
$1 - (1 - \hat p)^3$ = `r fmt(1 - (1 - p0)^3)`, so the surveys very nearly
census the occupied quadrats and there is little to correct. Set the simulator
to $p$ = 0.8 and $J$ = 3 to see the same thing; then set $p$ = 0.3 to see what
this analysis would look like for a cryptic species.

**Conditional occupancy of the undetected sites.** For an all-zero site the
model's posterior that it is occupied is $\psi(1-p)^J / [\psi(1-p)^J + 1 - \psi]$,
which under the null model is `r fmt(psi0 * (1 - p0)^3 / (psi0 * (1 - p0)^3 + 1 - psi0), 3)`
for a site with three surveys. Under `m2` each site has its own $\psi_i$ and
$p_{ij}$, and `ranef()` returns the site-level posterior of $z_i$.

```{r}
#| label: ranef
re  <- ranef(m2)
z_hat <- bup(re, stat = "mean")     # posterior mean of z_i
undetected <- rowSums(Y, na.rm = TRUE) == 0
summary(z_hat[undetected])
sum(undetected)
```

Every detected site has $z_i = 1$ with certainty. The undetected sites range
from essentially zero to about `r fmt(max(z_hat[undetected]))`, with the
highest values at mid-elevation forested quadrats where $\psi_i$ is high, and
at the quadrats with only one or two surveys, where $(1-p)^J$ is larger.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ranef
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Posterior probability that an undetected quadrat is occupied, against its elevation. Shape marks how many surveys it received."
sc <- siteCovs(umf)
df <- data.frame(elev = sc$elev, z_hat = z_hat,
                 n_surveys = factor(rowSums(!is.na(Y))),
                 detected = ifelse(undetected, "never detected", "detected"))
ggplot(subset(df, detected == "never detected"),
       aes(elev, z_hat, shape = n_surveys)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "#c08a1e") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("1" = 17, "2" = 15, "3" = 16), name = "surveys") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (standardised)", y = "P(occupied | all surveys zero)")
```

**Finite-sample against model occupancy.** Two different questions hide
behind "how many quadrats are occupied". The model parameter $\psi$ is the
probability a quadrat like these is occupied; the finite-sample quantity is
how many of *these* 237 quadrats are. The second is the sum of the $z_i$,
estimated by summing the posterior means, and its uncertainty is smaller
because the detected sites contribute no uncertainty at all.

```{r}
#| label: finite
c(naive_count = sum(!undetected),
  finite_sample = sum(z_hat),
  model_mean_psi_times_n = sum(predict(m2, "state")$Predicted))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-psi
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Predicted occupancy against elevation at mean forest cover, with the 95% confidence band. Ticks along the top are quadrats with a detection; along the bottom, quadrats without."
nd <- data.frame(elev = seq(min(sc$elev), max(sc$elev), length.out = 100),
                 forest = 0)
pr <- cbind(nd, predict(m2, "state", newdata = nd))
ggplot(pr, aes(elev, Predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "#1e8a5a", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1e8a5a", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_rug(data = subset(df, detected == "detected"), aes(x = elev, y = NULL),
           sides = "t", colour = "#1e8a5a", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_rug(data = subset(df, detected == "never detected"), aes(x = elev, y = NULL),
           sides = "b", colour = "#8a8c94", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (standardised)", y = expression(hat(psi)))
```

## Check

The MacKenzie and Bailey (2004) test compares the observed count of each
detection history (`000`, `001`, ..., `111`, with the two- and one-survey
cohorts separately) against what the fitted model expects, and bootstraps the
Pearson statistic from the model to get its reference distribution.
`AICcmodavg::mb.gof.test()` does it on an `unmarked` fit.

```{r}
#| label: gof
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
set.seed(2026)
gof <- mb.gof.test(m2, nsim = 200)
gof
```

```{r}
#| label: gof-vals
#| echo: false
chat <- gof$c.hat.est
```

The test rejects, with $\hat c$ = `r fmt(chat, 1)`. Two cells carry it:
`111` is observed well above its expectation, and `100` at about three times
its expectation, while the mixed histories `011` and `110` fall short. That
pattern is the signature of detection heterogeneity the covariates have not
captured. Some quadrats are easy, the bird is found every time, and some are
hard, so the histories bunch at the extremes rather than spreading
binomially. The excess of `100` could also be a closure failure: a bird
present and singing on the first visit that had moved on by the second.

Neither violation is harmless for $\hat\psi$. Unmodelled heterogeneity in $p$
means the all-zero sites are disproportionately the hard ones, where
$(1-p)^J$ is larger than the model thinks, so $\hat\psi$ is biased low.
Closure failure does the opposite: $\psi$ becomes the probability that a
quadrat was *used at some point* during the season, which is larger than the
probability it was occupied throughout, so $\hat\psi$ overstates the quantity
most people mean. Here the two may partly cancel, and with $\hat p$ near 0.8
the damage to $\hat\psi$ is bounded either way; a quasi-likelihood fix
multiplies the standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat c}$ = `r fmt(sqrt(chat), 1)`.
The constructive fixes are a detection covariate that captures the
heterogeneity, a finite-mixture detection model, or a dynamic model that
drops the closure assumption.

## The same model across the corpus

One table is a tutorial. The point of a warehouse is that the same six lines
run over every table of the same shape, so this section fits the null model
$\psi(\cdot)\,p(\cdot)$ to every species in every site-level detection or
count table in eco version 10 and asks three questions
of each fit: how far $\hat\psi$ sits from naive occupancy, whether the
estimate is at a boundary, and whether the MacKenzie and Bailey test rejects.
The tables are chosen by rule from `eco_metadata()`, not by name: site units,
a detection or count response, at least two occasions. Designs the model does
not describe (multi-scale eDNA, false-positive and two-scale co-occurrence
tables) are excluded by name, each with its reason, and the tables over the
100 MB that Redivis serves without a login are held back for now; both lists
are at the end of this section. The fits take most of an hour because
of the bootstrap, so they live in a companion script,
[`occupancy_corpus_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/occupancy_corpus_compute.R),
and the page reads its cache. Multi-season tables contribute the primary
period with the most surveys; count tables are collapsed to detection; a
species never detected in that period, or surveyed once per site, is skipped,
since the null model has nothing to fit or cannot separate $\psi$ from $p$.

```{r}
#| label: corpus-load
corpus <- readRDS("occupancy_data/occupancy_corpus.rds")
fits <- corpus$fits
fits$correction <- fits$psi - fits$naive
fits$boundary <- !fits$converged | fits$psi > 0.995 | fits$psi < 0.005 | fits$p < 0.005
# The test's cohort table has 2^J cells. Past ten surveys the expected counts
# are tiny and the statistic degenerates (the marten table, J = 24, returns a
# c-hat in the billions), so the test is only read where J <= 10.
fits[fits$J > 10, c("chisq", "gof_p", "c_hat")] <- NA
fits$reject <- !is.na(fits$gof_p) & fits$gof_p < 0.05
fits$floor <- ifelse(fits$sample_floor == "meets", "meets floor", "below floor")
```

```{r}
#| label: corpus-stats
#| echo: false
library(data.table)
f <- as.data.table(fits)
ct <- as.data.table(corpus$corpus_tables)
no_fit <- setdiff(ct[status == "fit", table], f$table)
n_fits <- nrow(f); n_tab <- uniqueN(f$table)
n_below <- uniqueN(f[floor == "below floor", table])
ok <- f[!boundary & floor == "meets floor"]
med_corr <- median(ok$correction); q_corr <- quantile(ok$correction, c(.1, .9))
share_reject <- mean(ok$reject[!is.na(ok$gof_p)])
med_chat <- median(ok$c_hat, na.rm = TRUE)
n_bound <- sum(f$boundary); n_bound_rare <- sum(f$boundary & f$naive < 0.05)
by_tab <- f[, .(n = .N, bound = sum(boundary), J = J[1]), by = table]
tb <- function(t, col) by_tab[table == t][[col]]
mhb_reject <- ok[table == "kery_2014_mhb_comm" & !is.na(gof_p), mean(reject)]
wt_chat <- f[table == "kery_2008_willowtit_occ", c_hat]
top <- ok[correction >= q_corr[2]]; top_n <- nrow(top)
top3_n <- top[table %in% c("bradferlawrence_2025_ukwood_beetle_comm", "maihoff_2023_berchtesgaden_bees_count",
                           "obrist_2024_gooseisland_birds_count"), .N]
medp <- function(t) median(ok[table == t, p])
n_rule <- nrow(ct); n_held <- sum(ct$status == "skipped"); n_excl <- sum(ct$status == "excluded")
n_eff_tab <- ct[status == "fit" & effort == "mapped", .N]
```

Of the `r n_rule` tables the rule selects, `r n_excl` are excluded by design
and `r n_held` held back for size, and the rule on one survey per site removes
`r length(no_fit)` more entirely
(`r paste0("\x60", no_fit, "\x60", collapse = " and ")`): in the period each
contributes, most sites were surveyed once for each species.

```{r}
#| label: corpus-groups
#| echo: false
grp <- f[, .(tables = uniqueN(table), species = .N,
             `at boundary` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(boundary)),
             `median p` = median(p[!boundary]),
             `median psi` = median(psi[!boundary]),
             `median psi - naive` = median(correction[!boundary]),
             `GOF rejects` = sprintf("%d / %d", sum(reject[!boundary]), sum(!is.na(gof_p[!boundary]))),
             `median c-hat` = median(c_hat[!boundary], na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(group = taxon_group)]
setorder(grp, -species)
gq <- function(g, col) grp[group == g][[col]]
knitr::kable(grp, digits = 2, caption = "The null model by taxon group. Medians and the test are over the fits not at a boundary.")
```

Across `r n_fits` species fits in `r n_tab` tables, `r n_bound` are at a
boundary, with $\hat\psi$ pinned to 1 or $\hat p$ to 0. A good share of those
(`r n_bound_rare`) are species detected at fewer than one site in twenty, where
a handful of detections cannot say whether the species is rare or merely hard
to see. The rest gather in a few designs: the extended Aldabra reef-fish
survey, with two visits per site and `r tb("koester_2023_aldabra_reeffishext_count", "bound")`
of `r tb("koester_2023_aldabra_reeffishext_count", "n")` species at the boundary;
the West Virginia camera grids, where the occasion is a single camera-day and
the per-day $\hat p$ for most species is under 0.01
(`r tb("clipp_2024_monongahela_comm", "bound")` of `r tb("clipp_2024_monongahela_comm", "n")`
species in the Monongahela table); and the Belgian carabid pitfalls, with
three visits and low catch rates. `r n_below` tables, most of them small
community surveys of reef fish, odonates and bumblebees, are below the
standard's sample floor. Among the well-behaved fits the median correction
$\hat\psi - \text{naive}$ is `r fmt(med_corr)`, with the middle 80% of species
between `r fmt(q_corr[1])` and `r fmt(q_corr[2])`. That upper decile is
species with $\hat p$ just above the boundary rule, and
`r top3_n` of its `r top_n` fits come from three tables: the UK woodland
beetle pitfalls, the Berchtesgaden wild bees and the Goose Island bird counts,
where the median $\hat p$ is `r fmt(medp("bradferlawrence_2025_ukwood_beetle_comm"))`,
`r fmt(medp("maihoff_2023_berchtesgaden_bees_count"))` and
`r fmt(medp("obrist_2024_gooseisland_birds_count"))`. Those fits are
technically interior and substantively the same failure as the boundary
ones.

The group table says the corpus has changed character. Birds were most of the
version 2 corpus; now invertebrates and fish together outnumber them.
Invertebrates are detected far less often than birds (median $\hat p$
`r fmt(gq("Invertebrates", "median p"))` against `r fmt(gq("Birds", "median p"))`)
and carry about twice the correction; fish are detected as often as birds but
estimated present at more of the sites. Whether that is the taxa or the designs that survey them (pitfalls and pan traps visited two or
three times, against point counts and territory mapping) the null model cannot
say, and the next section's covariate is a first attempt to tell them apart.

```{r}
#| label: fig-corpus
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-cap: "Estimated against naive occupancy for every species fit, one panel per taxon group. Colour is the estimated per-survey detection probability; open triangles are tables below the sample floor; points on the top edge are boundary fits. Hover a point for the species."
f$label <- sprintf("%s\n%s\n%d sites, J = %g\nnaive %.2f, psi %.2f, p %.2f%s",
                   f$table, f$taxon, f$n_sites, f$J, f$naive, f$psi, f$p,
                   ifelse(is.na(f$c_hat), "", sprintf("\nc-hat %.1f", f$c_hat)))
f$group <- factor(f$taxon_group, levels = grp$group)
g <- ggplot(f, aes(naive, psi, colour = p, shape = floor, text = label)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_point(size = 1.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#bfe3d2", high = "#0b4f33", name = "p", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("meets floor" = 16, "below floor" = 2), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 3) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Naive occupancy", y = "Estimated occupancy")
plotly::ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text", width = 760, height = 860) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(title = list(text = ""))) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The picture is the simulator's expected-naive line read backwards. Species
with high $\hat p$ sit on the diagonal; the correction grows as $\hat p$
falls, and below about $p = 0.2$ with three surveys the all-zero sites can no
longer be told apart from empty ones and the fit slides up the top edge. The
bird panel is mostly the first regime and the invertebrate panel mostly the
second. The below-floor tables show the same failure from the other direction:
ten or twenty sites cannot pin $\psi$ down whatever $p$ is.

```{r}
#| label: fig-corpus-gof
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The overdispersion estimate from the MacKenzie and Bailey test for every fit it could be run on (ten or fewer surveys, not at a boundary). Values above 10 are drawn at 10. The dashed line is 1, where the null model fits."
ggplot(f[!is.na(c_hat)], aes(pmin(c_hat, 10))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#1e8a5a", colour = "white", boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "#55575f") +
  labs(x = expression(hat(c)), y = "species")
```

The test rejects at the 5% level for `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_reject)`
of the well-behaved fits, with a median $\hat c$ of `r fmt(med_chat, 1)`. The
share tracks sample size and detection as a power calculation would predict:
in the MHB community table, with 266 quadrats and a median $\hat p$ above 0.6,
the test rejects for `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mhb_reject)` of species, while
in the low-$p$ invertebrate tables it rarely has the power to reject anything.
A quiet test there is not evidence of fit. That the willow tit's $\hat c$ of
`r fmt(wt_chat, 1)` is not unusual among the well-sampled bird tables is the
useful lesson: the constant-$p$ model is a starting point, and the detection
heterogeneity it leaves behind is the norm in field data, not a feature of one
table. The remedies are the ones listed above, and the covariates to try are
already in the tables' `unit_` and `obs_` columns.

```{r}
#| label: corpus-table
#| echo: false
tab <- f[, .(species = .N, group = taxon_group[1], sites = n_sites[1], J = J[1],
             `median p` = median(p, na.rm = TRUE),
             `median psi - naive` = median(correction, na.rm = TRUE),
             `at boundary` = sum(boundary),
             `GOF rejects` = sprintf("%d / %d", sum(reject), sum(!is.na(gof_p))),
             floor = floor[1]), by = table]
setorder(tab, -species)
```

<details><summary>Every table in the sweep (`r n_tab`), and the ones left out</summary>

```{r}
#| label: corpus-table-print
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
left_out <- ct[status != "fit" | table %in% no_fit,
               .(table, status = fifelse(table %in% no_fit, "no fit", status),
                 reason = fifelse(table %in% no_fit, "one survey per site per species in the period used", reason))]
knitr::kable(left_out)
```

</details>

### One covariate everywhere: effort on $p$

The null model's ĉ says the constant-$p$ assumption fails; the natural first
covariate is the one every protocol records in some form, how hard the survey
tried. `r n_eff_tab` of the tables in the sweep carry it: camera nights, days
or hours, minutes searched, the standardised survey intensity of the Swiss
transects, trap-nights at a station, pitfall traps or cover tiles per visit,
transect length. The units differ, so each is taken as standardised log effort
(the two Kéry tables are standardised already) and the model becomes
$\psi(\cdot)\,p(\text{effort})$. The slope is then the change in logit $p$ per
standard deviation of log effort, a comparable number across protocols. The
compute script fits it for every species in those tables, on the surveys with
an effort value, and reruns the goodness-of-fit test. Three tables the
metadata flags as having effort get no fit: in one the survey length is the
same at every survey, and in two the flagged column is not effort.

```{r}
#| label: effort-load
ef <- as.data.table(corpus$effort)
ef <- merge(ef, f[, .(table, taxon, n_sites, J, naive, p_null = p, c_hat_null = c_hat,
                      boundary, floor, taxon_group)], by = c("table", "taxon"))
ef[, `:=`(lo = slope - 1.96 * slope_se, hi = slope + 1.96 * slope_se,
          d_aic = aic_null - aic_effort)]
ef[, significant := converged & lo > 0]
ef[J > 10, c_hat_effort := NA]
ok_e <- ef[converged & !boundary]
```

```{r}
#| label: effort-table
#| echo: false
etab <- ok_e[, .(species = .N, effort = sub("^(obs|unit)_", "", effort_variable[1]),
                 `median slope` = median(slope),
                 `positive, CI excludes 0` = sprintf("%d / %d", sum(significant), .N),
                 `median delta AIC` = median(d_aic),
                 `median c-hat, null` = median(c_hat_null, na.rm = TRUE),
                 `median c-hat, effort` = median(c_hat_effort, na.rm = TRUE)), by = table]
setorder(etab, -species)
knitr::kable(etab, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: effort-stats
#| echo: false
n_e <- nrow(ok_e); n_pos <- sum(ok_e$slope > 0); n_sig <- sum(ok_e$significant)
n_neg <- sum(ok_e$hi < 0)
med_slope <- median(ok_e$slope)
both <- ok_e[!is.na(c_hat_null) & !is.na(c_hat_effort)]
share_improved <- mean(both$c_hat_effort < both$c_hat_null)
share_near_one <- mean(both$c_hat_effort <= 1.5)
es <- function(t) ok_e[table == t]
mya <- es("kyaw_2024_myanmar_mamm_comm"); mai <- es("maihoff_2023_berchtesgaden_bees_count")
clp <- ef[table %in% c("clipp_2024_monongahela_comm", "clipp_2024_wvprivate_comm")]
```

Of the `r n_e` species with a usable effort fit, `r n_pos` have a positive
slope, `r n_sig` have an interval above zero and `r n_neg` an interval below
it; the median slope is `r fmt(med_slope)` on the logit scale, so one standard
deviation more searching raises the odds of a detection by about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (exp(med_slope) - 1))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-effort
#| fig-cap: "The effort slope on logit p for every species, with 95% intervals, grouped by table. Filled points have an interval that excludes zero. Hover for the species."
ok_e[, table_short := sub("_(comm|occ|count|ves|nmix|dynocc)$", "", table)]
ok_e[, label := sprintf("%s\n%s\nslope %.2f (%.2f, %.2f)\np at mean effort %.2f\ndelta AIC %.1f%s",
                        table, taxon, slope, lo, hi, p_at_mean, d_aic,
                        ifelse(is.na(c_hat_effort), "", sprintf("\nc-hat %.1f -> %.1f", c_hat_null, c_hat_effort)))]
setorder(ok_e, table, slope)
ok_e[, row := seq_len(.N), by = table]
g <- ggplot(ok_e, aes(slope, row, text = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pmax(lo, -4), xmax = pmin(hi, 4)), height = 0, colour = "#8a8c94", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = significant), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = "#1e8a5a") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1e8a5a", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ table_short, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Effort slope on logit p (per SD of log effort)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
plotly::ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text", width = 760, height = 1000) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Three things stand out. The sign is mostly positive but the strength is not
uniform: where effort varies a lot between surveys the slope is large and the
fit improves sharply (the Hungarian pond searches, 3 to 114 minutes, with
eight of nine species positive and clear of zero; the Arkansas cameras, 1 to 7
days, ten of twelve; the Myanmar camera network, half a day to ten days per
occasion, `r sum(mya$significant)` of `r nrow(mya)` with a median $\Delta$AIC
of `r fmt(median(mya$d_aic), 1)`), while where it barely varies (the Los Lagos
stations, 67 to 80 trap-nights; the Chilean cameras, 2 to 5 nights) the slope
is unidentified and the interval spans zero. The MHB community table is the
instructive middle case: survey duration there runs from 105 to 420 minutes,
yet the median slope is small and the AIC gain is nil. The territory-mapping
protocol is designed so that every quadrat is covered completely on every
visit, and the extra minutes go to terrain and pace rather than to a more
thorough search, so for this protocol raw duration is not effort in the sense
the model wants. The willow tit and mallard tables carry the package's survey
intensity, effort scaled to the route, which is the better variable and the
reason those scripts kept it.

Two tables need a caveat before their slopes are read. In the West Virginia
camera grids the occasion is one camera-day and nearly every occasion is a
full 24 hours, so the slope rests on the few partial days at deployment and
retrieval, and `r sum(clp$boundary)` of `r nrow(clp)` species there are at a
boundary under the null model and drop out of the figure. In the
Berchtesgaden bee table the variable is whether a visit took one day or two,
and the slope is negative for `r sum(mai$slope < 0)` of `r nrow(mai)` species
(median `r fmt(median(mai$slope))`):
two-day visits detect less. That is not what effort does. One possible
reading, not yet checked against the deposit, is that a visit ran to a second
day when the first was cut short, so the variable marks bad conditions rather
than extra searching. It stays in
the sweep as a reminder that a column called effort has to be read against
the protocol before it goes into $p$.

And one covariate does not fix the fit: ĉ falls for
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_improved)` of the species where both tests
ran, but only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_near_one)` end up at or below
1.5, and the MHB median does not move. Most of the heterogeneity the null
model's test detected lives elsewhere, in the site, the observer, or the
abundance behind a collapsed count, which is where the `unit_` columns and a
mixture on $p$ come in.

## Where this goes

Everything above changes by one line in the state or observation process, and
eco carries a table for each.

- **Poisson state.** Let $N_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$ with
  $y_{ij} \mid N_i \sim \text{Binomial}(N_i, p)$ and the same table of counts
  fits the N-mixture model of chapter 6 (`unmarked::pcount()`).
  `eco_to_unmarked()` picks `pcount` when `y` goes beyond 0/1;
  `kery_2014_mhb_comm` is the MHB count table.
- **Markov state.** Let $z_{it}$ evolve across seasons by colonisation and
  extinction and the table with a `period` column fits the dynamic occupancy
  model of chapter 16 (`unmarked::colext()`), which is also the model that
  relaxes closure. `kery_2010_crossbill_dynocc` is the MHB crossbill table
  over nine years.
- **Species as random effects.** Give every species in a community table its
  own $(\psi_k, p_k)$ drawn from a shared distribution and you have the
  community occupancy model of chapter 11. `galvez_2021_araucania_comm` and
  `hamer_2024_hungary_amph_comm` are community tables with one period and
  several surveys; `eco_to_array()` keeps the species dimension that
  `eco_to_unmarked()` refuses.

## Reproducibility

Source: [`site/vignettes/occupancy.qmd`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/occupancy.qmd)
and [`occupancy_corpus_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/occupancy_corpus_compute.R)
in the eco repository; the corpus fits were run on `r corpus$date_run` with
`r corpus$nsim` bootstrap samples per test. Data were read with `eco_set_version(10)`, so a later
release of the warehouse does not change the page.

```{r}
#| label: versions
#| echo: false
v <- eco_version()
cat(sprintf("eco version %s (Redivis eco %s, eco_meta %s, released %s)\n",
            v$eco_version, v$eco, v$eco_meta, substr(v$released, 1, 10)))
cat(sprintf("R %s; eco %s; unmarked %s; AICcmodavg %s\n",
            getRversion(), packageVersion("eco"), packageVersion("unmarked"),
            packageVersion("AICcmodavg")))
```
